name: Kuba cloth and Kuba royal art
subtitle: Kuba cloth is handwoven from raffia palm fibre and embroidered or cut-pile decorated.

facts.label: What
facts.value: Kuba cloth is handwoven from raffia palm fibres, often embroidered, dyed or appliqued with geometric patterns after weaving.

facts.label: Who makes
facts.value: Men weave the ground cloth on a single-heddle loom; women do the decorative needlework.

facts.label: Who makes
facts.value: In Kuba culture, men cultivate the palms and weave the cloth, and women embroider the patterns.

facts.label: How
facts.value: Cut-pile: designs are stitched, then raffia fibre is drawn through with a needle and closely cut to make a dense pile.

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: Prestige cloths are joined into embroidered skirts worn by men and women at important ritual ceremonies including funerals.

facts.label: Uses
facts.value: Smaller panels are sold as yardage for clothing, currency and household furnishings.

facts.label: Currency
facts.value: Kuba cloth was historically used as a form of currency within Kuba society.

facts.label: Kingdom
facts.value: The Kuba kingdom was a federation of 18 ethnic groups ruled by the Bushong, whose royal court employed weavers, sculptors, metalsmiths and basket makers.

facts.label: Museum collections
facts.value: LACMA holds Kuba (Shoowa) ceremonial textile panels and skirts made in the late 19th-early 20th century.

parts.text: Kuba cloth is handwoven from raffia palm fibre and embroidered or cut-pile decorated. Men weave the ground cloth and women embroider it. Cloths served as dress at ceremonies and funerals, as signs of status and as currency, and are held by museums such as the V&A, LACMA and the Textile Museum.
